chapters.meaning: What changed: two Sunday developments on top of the morning's frame. First, the Beirut strike — Israel hit Beirut's southern suburbs Sunday, the first strike since June, killing Hezbollah chief of staff Haytham Tabtabai (Hezbollah confirmed; Lebanon health ministry: 5 killed, 25 wounded). The IDF told northern-Israel residents to continue daily routines — no Hezbollah military response anticipated as of now — but Hezbollah's political council says leadership is 'studying the matter of response,' so the escalation door is open. The four-beat read: (1) an Israeli strike decapitating Hezbollah's military staff inside Beirut, days before the Pope's Lebanon visit; (2) the surprise is the timing and the target — the first capital strike since June, aimed at the man Israel says led Hezbollah's rearmament; (3) against the benchmark of a fragile ceasefire under US pressure to disarm Hezbollah, this is escalation, not enforcement-as-usual; (4) for FX it is a haven-bid tailwind into Monday's open (JPY/CHF bid risk, the dollar's haven leg) — and it lands directly on the deal test, because Tehran insists the Lebanon front be part of any agreement, so today's strike complicates the very negotiations the deal needs. The one-question lens: does Hezbollah answer, or absorb it? Second, the signing test became claim day: Trump's camp says the deal is 'complete' (his social post: 'Deal with the Islamic Republic of Iran is now complete'), while Tehran's Sunday line is that negotiations have stalled and the Hormuz 7-day reopen offer is merely 'still on the table' (Araqchi, via Reuters Sunday). The four-beat read: (1) a claimed-complete deal vs a stalled negotiation — two incompatible stories in one morning; (2) the surprise is how thin the claim is — no Reuters/Bloomberg/CNBC/AP story of a signed deal or ceremony as of 4pm CT; (3) against the benchmark of June, when the same 'deal' narrative ran and collapsed, a claim without a signed text or Iranian confirmation is a headline, not an outcome — and the aggregator content screaming 'markets celebrate' is held, not used: its 'Brent $84.35' and 'WTI $81.65' would be ~20% drops off Friday's verified settles dressed up as ~3% ones; (4) for the dollar this keeps the soft-dollar weekend read intact — the deflation a real signing would bring hasn't materialized, and Beirut re-arms the haven bid. The one-question lens: has anything actually been signed, or is this another claim day? Thread: Friday had the Graham EO armed-but-unfired; Saturday corrected the tripwire into a 60-day review clock (~Dec 17) with no Trump decision; Sunday became claim day and escalation day. The rate thesis is untouched — October locked as a hold (~85%) into the Oct 27-28 blackout, December the debate (~74% for a hike), and the Fed stays silent. What it means: this morning's soft-dollar thesis holds — the signing deflation hasn't arrived, and Beirut adds a haven bid under Monday's open.

chapters.meaning: What changed: Sunday's ledger grew. (1) The Beirut strike — Israel's first on the capital since June, killing Hezbollah's chief of staff — is the escalation the deal test can't absorb quietly: Tehran insists the Lebanon front be part of any agreement, so the strike lands on the negotiations themselves. For crude this is a straight risk premium re-arm into the Sunday open. (2) The signing test is claim day, not done day: Trump's camp says the deal is 'complete' while Tehran says talks have stalled — no major wire carries a signed deal, and the aggregator 'markets celebrate' futures numbers don't survive arithmetic against Friday's verified settles (held, not used). The deflation a real signing would bring hasn't materialized. (3) Sunday's UKMTO ledger, carried as reported claims: a tugboat struck by two projectiles NE of Khor Fakkan, UAE (damaged but underway, one minor casualty — no vessel ID, no attribution), a 7-person skiff firing two shots at an LNG tanker off Yemen (turned away by armed security), and the Saudi-led coalition intercepting 2 Houthi ballistic missiles toward Khamis Mushait plus a drone toward Riyadh. Held, not priced: the IRGC mine claim (second wire, AFP, still zero independent confirmation), the Petersburg terminal damage (governor says 126+ UAVs downed, no fatalities — damage specifics conflict across outlets), and the stale-content trap — June's 'deal' articles are recrawling as fresh. Thread: Saturday's ledger — the record attack week (12 vessels, largest weekly UKMTO tally of the war, a new RPG-from-small-boat attack type), the IRGC's 'closed' declaration vs Cooper's 'controlled by the United States' rebuttal, the Petersburg strike, and Friday's Graham waiver that deflated the duties channel. What it means: the war premium now runs on two live engines — Hormuz (claims, still unpriced) and escalation (Beirut, freshly priced into the open). The ~$8.5 Brent-WTI spread from Friday's settles ($109.86 − $101.41) still reads as the world's tanker-risk price over the US benchmark — roughly double the normal ~$3-5 — and for FX it stays the CAD-vs-importers tell in one number.
